units: the clay delivered to the workshop loses its moisture too quickly
a body that is too dry breaks and the walls give way before the kiln
the craftsman wraps every block in a soaked cloth
the blocks are kept away from heat and from draughts
this treatment makes the body supple again and easy to throw
the dust that settles on damp pieces spoils the glaze
a sheet has been stretched above the shelves
the floor is damped before every throwing session
the vessels leave the kiln with a smooth, soft surface
the potter puts the success down to the care given to what surrounds the hand
text: The clay reaches the pottery workshop in dark blocks, and it gives up its moisture far too quickly. Worked too dry, the body crumbles beneath the fingers; the walls slump long before the kiln. The potter has answered with patience. He now wraps every block in a soaked cloth and sets it down in the shade, well out of the draught. The body softens again, yields to the palm, turns willingly on the wheel. One trouble still remains. Dust drifts onto the damp pieces and dulls the glaze. To keep it off, he has stretched a fine sheet above the shelves and damps the floor before each throwing session. The bowls then leave the kiln with a smooth, satin skin, warm to look at. Success, he says, rarely lies in the hand alone; it lies in the care given to everything that surrounds the hand.

units: the writer sets two ways of joining the timbers of a roof against each other
the traditional joint spreads the loads through the thickness of the wood
this joint grows tighter as it ages
fixing with bolts gathers the stresses around the holes
repeated shaking weakens the metal part
the argument from speed leaves out what later repairs cost
strength is measured by the ability to shift without snapping
experienced hands set a timber according to the way the tree grew
that judgement cannot be handed over to a machine
the writer judges a method by how long it serves
text: Set a roof frame cut with tenons and mortices beside one held together by bolts, and a badly framed argument comes clear. The jointed frame passes its loads through the whole thickness of the timber, takes up movement and grows tighter as it ages. The bolted frame gathers its stresses around the drilled holes, where steel turns brittle under repeated shaking. Speed of erection is the usual boast, and it leaves out what the later repairs cost. A strong joint is not the one that holds best through its first winter; it is the one that shifts without snapping. Carpenters trained the old way read the grain, keep clear of the knots, and set each timber the way the tree grew. No machine makes that call. Defending them is not nostalgia. It is admitting that a method is judged by how long it serves, not by how fast it goes up.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described works at bookbinding and is held by her fellows to be experienced
she learnt the trade beside a master who did not speak
that master corrected her way of working by moving her hands
her equipment includes bone tools, a sewing frame and presses of old timber
she uses skins, undyed cloth and papers marbled in a trough
she takes on two pupils every season
she picks them for their staying power rather than their skill
she holds that failure teaches more than success
she keeps her own early failures at home
her bindings are found in study collections and carry no name
text: The binder in question has worked at her bench for enough winters to be held by her fellows as a thoroughly seasoned hand. Her account falls into parts. Training first: years beside a master who never spoke, and who set her hands right by moving them. Then the equipment, bone folders, a sewing frame, presses whose knotted timbers groan at every turn of the screw. Then the materials: soft skins, undyed cloth, papers marbled in the trough. Teaching last, for she takes on two apprentices a season and picks them for their staying power rather than their neatness of hand. A failed binding, she holds, teaches far more than one that comes right, and she keeps her own early failures in a drawer at home. Her volumes pass through study libraries, and not one of them carries her name.

units: the visit follows the order its makers intended
the opening room shows unsharpened blades straight from the forge
the critic finds this first part plain and spare
the second section gathers tools that have been used
one cutting tool bears a nick left by a hard place in the wood
another tool shows an edge blunted by repeated use
the labels stay easy to follow without losing precision
the third room jumbles the trades together and confuses the visitor
the end of the visit shows silent images of hands at work
the verdict is favourable in spite of a weakening in the middle
text: An exhibition given over to cutting tools unfolds exactly in the order its makers intended. The opening room holds raw blades, straight from the forge and still black with scale; the argument is plain there, the staging spare. Next come the tools that have worked for a living, and the interest rises: a chisel nicked by a hard knot, a plane whose blunted iron speaks of thousands of passes. The labels keep clear of jargon without thinning the description. The third room disappoints. Cases are piled up, trades are jumbled together, and the thread so carefully laid out slips from the visitor's hand. The closing sequence partly recovers it, projecting hands at work in silence, with no music at all. One leaves persuaded by the whole demonstration, in spite of a marked hollow at the centre of the route.

units: the writer answers a question about how well his workshop is running
the seat he made would not stand level
the cause lies in a joint driven home into timber that was not dry enough
the shrinking of the wood as it dried loosened the joint
the writer took the whole piece apart
a craftsman nearby had warned him
he let the wood dry for a whole season before making it again
the joints hold now and the surface comes up smooth easily
he blames his own hurry rather than any lack of skill
he asks to borrow a hollow tool because his own is finished
text: You ask whether the workshop is running properly at last, so I had better be straight with you. The stool I put together over the winter wobbled, and it wobbled because I drove the tenons home into timber that was still damp. As the leg dried it shrank, the joint worked loose, and the thing ended up limping. So I pulled it all apart. The old joiner in the shed next door had warned me, and this time I let the boards breathe for a whole season before starting again. The joints hold now, and the surface I left rough after the first sanding comes up smooth with hardly any effort. It was my hurry that beat me, far more than my skill. If you come this way, bring your curved gouge. Mine has given up and I daren't hollow a seat without one. Write soon, and tell me whether your kiln is drawing.

units: a guild of weavers sees its plantations failing
the shoots they cut have grown shorter and snap during shaping
worn-out ground is held to blame
cutting that comes round too often tires the stools of the plant
the plots are now worked at longer intervals
organic matter is worked into the ground
older and suppler varieties have been put back into cultivation
output dropped by a third in the first season and then climbed again
the spokesman of the group grants a rise in the price of the objects sold
the collective hands on to beginners a way of cutting that was almost abandoned
text: What becomes of a trade when its raw material runs short? Put to a guild of basket weavers whose beds of willow are failing, the question drew an answer in three movements. The finding first: the rods they cut come up shorter now, and they snap under the weave. Then the diagnosis, worn-out ground and cutting that comes round too often for the stools to recover. Then the correction, two seasons old: longer rotation between the plots, compost worked in, older and suppler varieties put back into the ground. Output dropped by a third in the first season and has since climbed again, their spokesman explains. Asked about the price of a basket, he grants the rise and stands by it, since lasting work costs what it costs. The group now teaches beginners how to cut, a skill almost no workshop was still handing on.

units: a stoneworker teaches his pupil that every block calls for its own hand
the first stone is coarse in texture and full of hard grains
that stone rings brightly when it is struck
the second stone is softer and comes off with a smooth finish
the pupil wants to know which of the two is the better
the master refuses to weigh one material directly against the other
he holds that only the intended use can settle it
the coarse stone suits a step because it does not slip
the smooth stone suits a sill because water runs off it
the master foretells that the pupil will one evening stop asking
text: The stonemason was explaining patiently to his apprentice that no two blocks laid side by side ever call for the same hand. The first, he said, is coarse, full of hard grains that catch the punch and ring bright under the mallet. The second is softer, gives itself up to the drag and comes off satin, almost kind to the palm. The apprentice then asked which was the better stone of the two. There is no sense in the question, the mason answered: you do not weigh one material against another, you weigh what is wanted of them. A stair tread wants the coarse block, which will not slip under a boot; a window sill takes the other, which water washes and leaves. Then he added, wiping the white dust from his forearms, that the lad would choose for himself on the evening he stopped asking.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the changes in the metal casting shops are set out strand by strand
charred wood was given up for a denser fuel
that change raised the heat reached in the vessels
the air devices were at first worked by arm
they were later driven by the force of water
this mechanisation made the heating steady
rammed sand took the place of clay for forming the impressions
this material stands changes of heat better and draws away without cracking
a measured addition of tin gave a metal that took knocks better
a post for watching the furnace appeared and cut into the founder's authority
text: To follow the history of the metal casting shops properly, one has to take the strands apart. The fuel to begin with: charred wood gave way to denser coals, and the heat in the vessels climbed with it. Then the bellows, at first pumped by arm alone, later swung by wheels that running water turned, which made the heating steady. The moulds too: rammed sand took the place of raw clay, since it stands the sudden changes of heat better and draws away without cracking. And the alloys, where a measured dose of tin yielded a metal less brittle, able to ring without flying apart. Every one of these gains rearranged the division of the work itself. The founder gave up part of his authority to the man who watched and set the furnace, a post that had existed in none of these shops before.

units: the worker lifts a quantity of molten glass on the end of his iron
that mass is almost runny at the moment it is taken up
it is rolled along a metal surface to bring it true and firm the outside
blowing air opens a cavity inside the mass
brief reheats alternate with spells of shaping
glass that has gone too cold splits at the smallest knock
the opening at the top is widened with a pair of jaws
the piece is then handed to an assistant
a last stay in an oven brings the heat down by stages through the night
without that gradual cooling the object would break of itself
text: The glassblower begins by dipping his iron into the molten bath and lifting out a thick orange gather, so nearly liquid that it hangs by its own weight alone. He rolls it along a steel plate to bring it true and firm the outside. Then the first breath: a bubble opens in the heart of the mass and widens as the air presses. From here he works in turns, brief reheats against spells of shaping, for glass that has lost its heat grows brittle and splits at the smallest knock. Once the belly is right, he flares the neck with a pair of jaws, frees the piece and hands it to an assistant. The last stage belongs to the annealing oven, where the heat comes down by stages through the night. Without that measured descent, the strains inside would burst the object as it stood quietly on a shelf.

units: a damaged drain let water through above a gilding workshop
the store room was reached by the leak
the fine metal leaves kept there are extremely light
the paper sheets between them buckled under the damp
the leaves welded together and became unusable
the shortage of supplies halted the repair of an old frame
the woman who placed the order saw her date pushed back
the accident had consequences for three other trades
the store was moved down low and shut into a cupboard
a notebook now records the state of each batch every time it is opened
text: A split length of gutter above the gilding workshop was enough to upset a whole season. Water crept into the store, where beaten leaves of gold lay sleeping, so thin that a breath will carry them off. The damp buckled the tissue papers that kept the sheets apart, and the sheets welded together, good for nothing at all. With no stock to hand, the gilder had to break off the repair of an old frame, which pushed back her client's order, and the client in her turn was working to a date. Step by step the accident reached a joiner, a varnisher and a carrier. Out of it the gilder drew a rule she keeps to now: the store has come down to floor level, into a shut cupboard, and a notebook records the state of each batch every time it is opened. The roof still leaks, but the gold sleeps dry.
